input: Liquid-liquid extraction can be used to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) for this system is 2.6 at 25 °C, and the design is based on 3 countercurrent stages. On this basis, the predicted recovery is 98% of the acetic acid present in the feed. A distribution coefficient of 2.6 means that the majority of the acid passes into the organic phase at equilibrium in each stage, and the use of 3 countercurrent stages compounds this effect, since the aqueous stream comes into contact with progressively leaner solvent as it moves through the stages, causing the amount of acid remaining in the raffinate to fall at every stage. The countercurrent arrangement is central to this behaviour, since it ensures that the freshest solvent is brought into contact with the most depleted aqueous stream at the raffinate end of the cascade, thereby maintaining a driving force for transfer along the whole length of the equipment rather than allowing it to vanish at one end. The figure of 98% is the result returned by the equilibrium-stage calculation based on these two inputs. It should be noted, however, that the prediction relies on two important assumptions, namely that the stages reach equilibrium and that the mutual solubility of the solvents is negligible, and neither of these assumptions has yet been checked on the actual solvents. Until both assumptions have been verified, the recovery of 98% should therefore be regarded as an equilibrium-stage estimate rather than as a demonstrated performance. In practice, both effects would be expected to move the achieved recovery away from the predicted value, and pilot or laboratory measurements on the actual solvent pair would be needed before the design figure could be relied upon.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent, with a predicted recovery of 98% of the acetic acid in the feed. The prediction rests on a distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) of 2.6 at 25 °C and a design of 3 countercurrent stages. A coefficient of 2.6 places most of the acid in the organic phase at equilibrium in each stage, and 3 countercurrent stages compound that split: the aqueous stream meets progressively leaner solvent as it passes through the stages, so the acid left in the raffinate falls at every stage. Countercurrent flow is what makes the leanest solvent meet the most depleted aqueous stream, holding a concentration difference open at the raffinate end of the cascade. The 98% is the figure the equilibrium-stage calculation returns on those two inputs. The recovery is stated against the acid in the feed: it is the share of the incoming acid that leaves in the organic product, and the share that remains leaves with the raffinate, so the figure also fixes what the raffinate still carries. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents. The first assumption sets the recovery the stages can reach, because a stage that leaves before equilibrium transfers less acid than the coefficient promises. The second sets whether the phases keep their compositions, because solvents that dissolve in each other change both the phase volumes and the coefficient itself. Recovery on the actual solvents is therefore unsettled until both assumptions are tested, and the 98% stands as the equilibrium-stage estimate, not as a measured performance.
